title: The Great Big Door That Would Not Open

topics.value_lesson: Trying a different way is how fixes are found — each wrong try teaches something

spine: We arrive at a friendly castle to meet the smiling knight, but the great big door is stuck, and each wrong try teaches us how to open it.

segments.text: We are going to visit Sir Cedric. He is a knight, and his castle is big and round and friendly, with a grassy path right up to the door. We walk and walk. Listen. Jingle, jingle. That is Sir Cedric's armor, somewhere inside! The great big door has a round iron ring. We stand on tiptoe. We lift it. Knock, knock, knock! We put our ears to the wood. No footsteps. The door is stuck fast.

"Our ideas first!" we say. We push the door with our hands. Push, push! It does not move. But under our palms, the wood leans out. Out! "It opens the other way!" we say. We put our fingers on the round iron ring and pull. Pull, pull! Still stuck. But the ring turns a little in our hands. Click. Oh! A tiny click. "Did you hear that?" we whisper. The ring turns! That is the clue. The door wants us to turn it.

"Somebody who knows!" we say. "Who knows this old door's secrets?" Up above the door, a little window opens. An old lady leans out and waves. "Hullo, little ones!" she calls. "That old door never opens for pushing or pulling. Only for turning the ring and lifting the latch." Down she climbs, and she shows us where her hands go. "Like this," she says. "Now you try."

Now we know what to do! We stand on tiptoe. We take the round iron ring. We turn it. We lift it. Click! The great big door swings open. Creeeak! Sir Cedric kneels down, down, down to us. He lifts his shiny visor. Click! Underneath is a big smile, and a wink. "You did it!" he says. "What did you find out there?" And Watson the castle cat twirls around our legs. Purr, purr. He leads us into the sunny courtyard.

Watson trots to the kitchen. Cook Margery waves us in. The bread dough is big and puffy! "Give it a squish," she says. We push it down. Squish! It sighs, soft as a pillow. She bakes it warm and saves us the end piece. We curl up in the wide stone window seat. Watson purrs on our lap. The bread is soft and warm in our hands. Sir Cedric tucks a little round loaf in our pocket. "For the walk home," he says.

Sir Cedric's armor jingles as we follow him to the stable. His horse Pip is big and gentle. "Hold your hand flat, like a little table," says Sir Cedric. We hold out three apple pieces. One, two, three! Pip snuffles them up, soft and tickly. Old Nan shows us the great wooden beam. We help slide it across the door. Boom! The door shuts happy and snug. Watson purrs. Pip gives us a soft whiskery nuzzle. "For remembering," says Sir Cedric.

gathered_but_unused: Castle doors were made of thick, heavy wood, sometimes oak, so they could be strong and last a long time.
Real castles had a gatehouse — a little room built right over the big doorway where guards could wave hello to visitors.
Drawbridges were bridges that could lift up and lower down over a ditch of water called a moat.
Knights wore shining armor made of metal rings and plates that jingled when they walked.
Castles had tall towers where people could look out and see far across the fields.
Some castle windows were narrow slits on the outside but wide on the inside, so the window seat was big enough to sit in.
People in castles kept animals nearby — horses in stables, chickens in the yard, and sometimes falcons.
Castles had big kitchens with huge fireplaces where cooks made bread and soup for everyone inside.
